description: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced. A height-balanced tree is one where the depths of the two subtrees of every node never differ by more than one.
intuition: Instead of checking balance at each node from the top down (which recalculates heights repeatedly), work from the bottom up. As you compute each subtree's height, check if the left and right heights differ by more than 1. If any subtree fails, propagate a "broken" signal (-1) upward to stop early.
approach: Use a bottom-up DFS that returns the height of each subtree. If any subtree is unbalanced, propagate -1 upward to short-circuit. This avoids recalculating heights repeatedly.
jsWalkthrough:
root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]
Tree:     3
         / \
        9  20
           / \
          15   7

height(3):
  leftHeight  = height(9) = 1  (balanced)
  rightHeight = height(20):
    leftHeight  = height(15) = 1
    rightHeight = height(7)  = 1
    |1-1| = 0 <= 1 -> return 2
  |1-2| = 1 <= 1 -> return 3
height(root) = 3, not -1 -> return true

Unbalanced example: [1,2,null,3]
  height(1): left=height(2): left=height(3)=1, right=0, |1-0|=1 ok -> 2
  right=height(null)=0, |2-0|=2 > 1 -> return -1
height(root) = -1 -> return false
explanation:
- height() returns the actual height of a balanced subtree, or -1 if it's unbalanced.
- For each node, compute left and right heights. If either is -1, propagate -1 (unbalanced).
- If the difference between left and right heights exceeds 1, return -1.
- Otherwise, return the true height: 1 + max(left, right).
- The top-level call just checks if the result is -1 (unbalanced) or not.
hints: A naive approach computes height at each node, leading to O(n^2). Can you do it in O(n)?
Compute height bottom-up. If any subtree is unbalanced, return a sentinel value.
Use -1 as a sentinel meaning "unbalanced" to short-circuit early.

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: n = tree nodes; h = tree height.

phases.label: Visit nodes and follow child links
Compare child heights and return a height or −1

timeComplexityBreakdown.note: Each subtree’s height is computed at most once. An unbalanced result may stop recursion earlier.

complexityVariables.n: Number of nodes in the tree
